reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics; Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Maternal PKU syndrome is a teratogenic embryopathy: the fetus is harmed by transplacental phenylalanine from a mother with poorly controlled phenylketonuria, not by an inherited enzyme defect in the child, who is usually a heterozygous carrier and biochemically normal.

The classic tetrad in the offspring is microcephaly, congenital heart disease, intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, and intellectual disability, often with a characteristic facial appearance resembling foetal alcohol syndrome.

Phenylalanine is actively concentrated across the placenta, so fetal levels exceed maternal levels; the threshold for damage is lower than that for classical PKU brain injury, meaning even mildly elevated maternal levels can be teratogenic.

Congenital heart defects, particularly coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy of Fallot and other conotruncal and left-sided lesions, arise from first-trimester exposure, so metabolic control must be achieved BEFORE conception, not merely once pregnancy is recognised.

Preconception counselling and reinstitution of a strict phenylalanine-restricted diet with medical protein (phenylalanine-free amino acid mixture) is the cornerstone; many adult women previously told they could relax diet must resume it well before attempting to conceive.

Adherence is a major problem because many women diagnosed by newborn screening discontinued diet in childhood ('diet for life' was not historically advised) and find the restricted diet difficult; structured multidisciplinary metabolic and obstetric care improves outcomes.

Tyrosine becomes conditionally essential and must be supplemented, and tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin) responsiveness should be assessed as it can aid control in selected women; overtreatment causing maternal phenylalanine deficiency also harms the fetus.
Because affected offspring do not have PKU themselves, a normal newborn screen in the baby does not exclude maternal PKU embryopathy; the diagnosis rests on maternal history and biochemistry.
reference.pathophysiology: Phenylketonuria results from deficiency of hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor), causing accumulation of phenylalanine. In pregnancy, phenylalanine is actively transported across the placenta and concentrated in the fetal compartment, so an inadequately treated affected mother exposes the developing embryo and fetus to sustained hyperphenylalaninaemia. Excess phenylalanine is directly neurotoxic and disrupts organogenesis: it impairs neuronal proliferation and migration and interferes with the metabolism of other large neutral amino acids and neurotransmitter precursors. First-trimester exposure disturbs cardiac neural crest and outflow-tract development, producing congenital heart disease, while ongoing exposure impairs brain growth and myelination, yielding microcephaly and intellectual disability, and restricts somatic growth. The severity of fetal damage correlates closely with the level and duration of maternal blood phenylalanine, especially periconceptional and first-trimester control; the fetus is affected regardless of its own genotype, being typically an unaffected carrier.
additionalDifferentials: foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (overlapping facies, microcephaly, growth restriction and cardiac defects)
congenital infections of the TORCH group causing microcephaly and growth restriction
other teratogen embryopathies (anticonvulsants such as valproate, warfarin, retinoids)
primary (non-maternal) inherited metabolic disease in the infant
constitutional or placental-insufficiency intrauterine growth restriction
tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor disorders in the mother mimicking classical PKU control problems
additionalInvestigations: serial maternal blood phenylalanine and tyrosine monitoring before and throughout pregnancy
confirmation of maternal PKU genotype/phenotype and tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin) responsiveness testing
detailed fetal anomaly ultrasound and fetal echocardiography
serial fetal growth scans and monitoring of head circumference
maternal nutritional assessment including protein, vitamin B12, iron and micronutrient status on restricted diet
paediatric developmental and cardiac assessment of the neonate
exclusion of foetal alcohol exposure and congenital infection where the phenotype overlaps
redFlags: unplanned pregnancy or conception occurring while maternal phenylalanine is poorly controlled
persistently elevated maternal blood phenylalanine during the first trimester
fetal microcephaly, growth restriction or a structural cardiac anomaly detected on antenatal imaging
maternal phenylalanine driven too low, risking amino-acid deficiency and fetal catabolic harm
loss to follow-up of a woman of childbearing age with known PKU no longer on diet
reference.prognosis: When strict maternal metabolic control is achieved before conception and maintained throughout pregnancy, the risk of the embryopathy falls markedly and offspring outcomes approach those of the general population. Poor periconceptional and first-trimester control carries high rates of microcephaly, congenital heart disease, growth restriction and irreversible intellectual disability in the child.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal newborn screen in the baby excludes harm; the offspring is usually an unaffected carrier yet may be severely damaged by intrauterine phenylalanine exposure.
Achieving metabolic control only after pregnancy is confirmed, by which time cardiac organogenesis and early neurodevelopment have already occurred.
Allowing women diagnosed in infancy to remain off diet without preconception planning, on the outdated view that diet can be stopped after childhood.
Overzealous restriction causing maternal phenylalanine deficiency, which itself impairs fetal growth and development.
Neglecting tyrosine and micronutrient supplementation and dietetic support, leading to maternal malnutrition on the restricted diet.
references: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, current edition
Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
van Wegberg et al. European guidelines on the diagnosis and management of phenylketonuria (Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases)
management: Preconception reinstitution of a strict phenylalanine-restricted diet with a phenylalanine-free amino-acid substitute, achieving target maternal levels before conception rather than after pregnancy is recognised
Frequent maternal blood phenylalanine and tyrosine monitoring before and throughout pregnancy with dietary titration
Sapropterin, a tetrahydrobiopterin analogue, in documented responders as an adjunct to dietary control
Maternal nutritional support ensuring adequate protein, tyrosine, vitamin B12, iron and micronutrients on the restricted diet
Detailed foetal anomaly ultrasound, foetal echocardiography and serial growth and head-circumference scans to detect embryopathy such as congenital heart disease, microcephaly and growth restriction
Neonatal paediatric developmental and cardiac assessment after delivery
Structured multidisciplinary metabolic and obstetric care with adherence support and genetic counselling
